extracted.intended_audience: general readers and contemporary newspaper readers interested in the Maria Monk controversy, evidence and press disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and primary-source material about how to judge the truth of sensational allegations published in the press (affidavits, certificates, editorial replies), focused on the Maria Monk/Hotel Dieu controversy. Emphasizes what counts as credible evidence, how to test allegations, and norms of publication and reply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affidavit / sworn testimony credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Sworn affidavits and depositions (taken 'on the Holy Evangelists' and before a Justice of the Peace) are presented as formal evidence; their probative weight depends on how they were made and what they assert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether testimony is sworn and before a proper official (e.g., 'Sworn before me ... W. ROBERTSON, J. P.'), whether it is firsthand or hearsay (the text criticizes hearsay: 'His evidence on this point is merely hearsay'), the witness's ability to sign (e.g., 'signed with a cross'), and whether statements are internally consistent or contradictory. The page gives examples of affidavits being questioned because they contain hearsay, contradict other evidence, or are signed by witnesses unable to write; these factors reduce their credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration / independent confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple independent witnesses and confirmations from 'persons of respectability' increase the likelihood that published allegations are true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concurrence across unrelated witnesses and for certificates of belief by reputable subscribers (e.g., the certificate: 'We the subscribers... have no hesitation in declaring our belief in the truth of the statements'). The publishers emphasize that 'several intelligent and disinterested persons had satisfied themselves by much examination that it was true' and point to spontaneous witnesses offering testimony as strengthening the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical/site inspection as decisive test
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct physical inspection or opening of the alleged site (the Hotel Dieu Nunnery) is presented as the only fair and conclusive test to settle factual disputes about what occurred there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publishers repeatedly assert that 'the only fair test--the opening of the Nunnery' would settle 'Is our book true or false?' They argue that affidavits and outside opinion are secondary to direct inspection of the institution and its records: 'By the issue of this investigation... then, and not till then, will the great question be settled.' Use of on-site or institutional inspection is recommended when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / plagiarism as an undermining factor
rubrics_metrics.description: If an exposé is substantially copied from an earlier work ('word for word and letter for letter'), allegations of originality and therefore credibility are undermined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text documents an accusation that the book was copied from 'The Gates of Hell opened' and describes publisher responses (offer of $100 reward to show resemblance). Assessors should check prior publications for near-verbatim matches; demonstration of copying weakens claims that the work reports fresh, local facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial fairness and right of reply
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers and editors are judged on whether they give accused parties or authors the opportunity to answer charges; refusal to publish replies is an editorial failure bearing on how the public can judge contested claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The publishers complain that replies were refused ('the editor of the N. Y. Catholic Diary... declined' to publish their letter) and that many papers were 'almost entirely closed against every thing in her defence.' When evaluating press disputes, consider whether rebuttals and inquiries were given a fair chance to appear in the same venues where accusations were printed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source bias, motive, and partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The political, religious, or personal motives of witnesses, editors, and publishers affect how much weight to give their statements; identifiably hostile or partisan sources may be 'polluted' and less reliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights charges that some evidence came from 'a polluted source' or 'avowedly hostile' parties and cautions readers to account for such bias. Conversely, statements by respected ministers or civic leaders are used to bolster claims. Assessors should weigh potential motives (religious antagonism, desire to discredit opponents) when judging testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility, reasonableness, and coherence
rubrics_metrics.description: Allegations should be judged against 'reason or common sense' and internal coherence; improbable or inconsistent accounts are suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Father McMahon argues the scandalous production is 'no way consonant to reason or common sense.' The publishers likewise point out contradictions in the Montreal affidavits. Use logical assessment: check whether timelines, stated movements, and claims about who knew what are coherent and plausible given geography, time, and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer judicial/legal inquiry for contested facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters of contested fact are best resolved through formal legal or judicial processes (court inquiry, sworn examination) rather than solely through newspapers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly references attempts and appeals to 'legal investigation' and 'what testimony is intended' being testimony 'legally given.' It emphasizes that presenting testimony before a court or opening the Nunnery are proper routes to establish facts. When evaluating contested public accusations, prefer evidence produced under legal procedures because of their formal safeguards (oaths, cross-examination, official record).
